 Chapter 1: Executive Summary
Virginia Electric and Power Company (“Dominion Energy” or the “Company”), headquartered in Richmond, Virginia,
is a vertically integrated utility serving approximately 2.8 million electric customers across 30,000 square miles in
Virginia and North Carolina. The Company operates generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure to
deliver on our mission to provide reliable, affordable, and increasingly clean energy to power our customers every
day. This responsibility requires Dominion Energy to plan for customers’ needs across the entire electric system,
from the resources that produce electricity, to the high-voltage network that moves it across the region, to the local
facilities that deliver it to homes and businesses.
Dominion Energy’s Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) is a 20-year reliability planning document filed annually with
the Virginia State Corporation Commission (“SCC”) and the North Carolina Utilities Commission (“NCUC”). This
year, the Company files a full comprehensive IRP in North Carolina and an interim update in Virginia (collectively,
the “2026 IRP”). The 2026 IRP evaluates how a range of scenarios could meet customers’ future energy and
capacity needs under different assumptions while complying with applicable state and federal laws and regulations,
public policy requirements, market conditions, and other guidelines. The IRP is not a request to approve a specific
project, resource portfolio, or cost recovery. Rather, it provides regulators and stakeholders with a transparent,
scenario-based assessment of potential pathways to meet growing customer demand. The Company’s IRP is based
on a “snapshot in time” utilizing current technologies, market information, and projections.
The 2026 IRP focuses on the continuing trends seen in demand forecasts, federal and state policy affecting
planning assumptions, and capacity market conditions within PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and how these
contribute to near- and long-term planning for the Company.
Electricity demand forecasts for the Dominion Energy delivery Zone of PJM (“DOM Zone”) continue to increase,
while the timing of demand is changing (i.e., recent system peaks occurring during winter mornings and summer
evenings, when output from weather-dependent resources may be limited). At the same time, new generation and
transmission projects face longer development timelines, interconnection constraints, supply-chain pressures, and
permitting and local siting challenges. Together, these conditions require flexible planning and a diversified portfolio
with an “all of the above” approach that is capable of serving customers during all hours and seasons.
The 2026 IRP contemplates the substantially expanded energy storage objectives signed into Virginia law this year.
Dominion Energy must petition for approval to construct or acquire 16,000 megawatts (“MW”) of short-duration
storage by 2045, including 4,000 MW by the end of 2030. The legislation also establishes conditional targets for
4,000 MW of long-duration storage, subject to an SCC determination that the technologies are technically viable and
the targets are reasonably achievable. In addition, Virginia resumed participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas
Initiative (“RGGI”) in July 2026, requiring the Company to account for emissions allowances and associated costs in
its planning and operations. The IRP evaluates these policy requirements alongside practical considerations such as
technology maturity, deliverability, development schedules, and customer cost.
Changes in the PJM market further shape this IRP. Dominion Energy participates in PJM’s capacity market to
satisfy a portion of its resource adequacy obligations. Recent auctions demonstrate a tightening regional supply-
demand balance as seen with the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction clearing at the federally approved price cap
and total committed capacity remaining more than 6,800 MW below PJM’s reliability requirement. The auction
achieved a 14.4% installed reserve margin compared with PJM’s 20% target. The 2028/2029 auction marked the
second consecutive Base Residual Auction to clear below PJM’s reliability requirement, highlighting growing
resource adequacy challenges across the region. These results reflect many factors including load growth,
retirement of dispatchable generation, delays in bringing replacement resources online, and changes in Effective
Load Carrying Capability (“ELCC”) accreditation that more closely measure how resources perform during periods of
system stress.



                                                           3
 These market conditions have direct implications for planning assumptions incorporated into this IRP. Dominion
Energy relied on market purchases for approximately 20% to 23% of energy served from 2021 through 2025, and
this number continues to grow. Market purchases will remain an important resource, but increasing dependence on
external supply increases customers’ exposure to price volatility, transmission congestion, and the risk that sufficient
power may not be available when it is needed most. That risk is particularly acute during extreme weather or other
periods of regional stress, when neighboring systems face the same extreme weather or resource constraints and
have limited surplus available to export. In addition, the capacity market’s three-year forward structure may not
provide sufficient lead time or long-term revenue certainty to support development of capital-intensive dispatchable
resources. Accordingly, the 2026 IRP emphasizes adding and retaining accredited capacity within the DOM Zone to
reduce overreliance on external supply, while continuing prudent participation in PJM’s energy and capacity
markets.
The Company’s Near-Term Reliability Plan responds to these conditions with a broad set of actions already
underway or in development. The Plan includes completion of the 2,600 MW Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project,
which began delivering power to the grid in 2026; development of approximately 1,617 MW of solar across 19
projects expected to be completed by 2030; continued deployment of short-duration storage; and testing of
emerging long-duration storage technologies at Darbytown Power Station. Dominion Energy is also advancing a
new natural gas-fired resource expected to enter service by June 2029 and soliciting proposals from a competitive
request for up to 7.3 GW of dispatchable generation with potential in-service dates through 2036.
While the IRP focuses on long-term planning, it is based on the foundation of near-term reliability actions. Dominion
Energy is pursuing transmission expansion and grid-enhancing technologies to improve deliverability and reduce
constraints; maintaining and optimizing existing generating units; expanding power purchase agreements; and
implementing approved demand-side management programs. These programs are projected to reduce energy
requirements by 1,601 GWh and summer capacity needs by 390 MW in 2026, growing to 2,956 GWh and 996 MW,
respectively, by 2031. The Company is also preparing to launch its Virtual Power Plant (“VPP”) pilot, which will test
the coordinated use of customer-owned batteries, electric vehicles, smart thermostats, and other distributed
resources as flexible grid assets.
The Company presents 17 modeling scenarios in this 2026 IRP, including three primary portfolios, four
Commission/Staff Directed cases, two additional cases, and eight sensitivities based on distinct market scenarios.
Together, these analyses test different assumptions about load growth, retirements, storage deployment, fuel and
construction costs, policy requirements, and resource availability. The Company Preferred Plan reflects a balanced
strategy that combines dispatchable generation, renewable resources, storage, demand-side programs,
transmission and distribution investments, power purchase agreements, and market purchases. This diversity is
essential because no single resource can satisfy all customer needs across every hour, season, and operating
condition.
The central conclusion of the 2026 IRP is that reliable service in a rapidly changing environment requires timely
action and flexibility. Load growth, PJM resource adequacy concerns, public policy requirements, and infrastructure
development constraints are converging at a pace that increases the priority on successful execution of the plan.
Dominion Energy’s planning approach therefore preserves multiple resource options, reduces overreliance on any
one technology or the wholesale market, and recognizes the need to align generation, transmission, distribution,
and customer resources. Through disciplined execution and continued engagement with regulators and
stakeholders, the Company will remain focused on meeting customers’ growing needs while managing affordability
and advancing an increasingly clean and resilient electric system.

 Chapter 2: Overview of the 2026 IRP

2.1 What is the IRP?
The IRP is a long‑range, 20‑year reliability planning document that is filed in both Virginia and North Carolina. It
provides a structured, analytical way to evaluate how customer energy needs could be met over time by testing
assumptions, constraints, and different resource portfolios. The analysis conducted for this IRP is a “snapshot in
time” that focuses on reliability, affordability, environmental factors, and system considerations under current laws
and across a range of potential future conditions.
While IRP assumptions and inputs are gathered to satisfy a defined statutory and regulatory framework for each
filing, requirements continue to evolve as legislation, commission orders, and market rules change.
The IRP serves as a tool that helps the Company, its regulators, and other stakeholders assess potential scenarios
for maintaining reliable and affordable electric service while evaluating opportunities to meet future energy needs.
Through the IRP process, the Company examines a range of assumptions and resource options to identify portfolios
that can support customers over a 20-year planning horizon. This planning approach enables the Company to
consider both current system requirements and future uncertainties as it evaluates potential investments and
operational strategies.
To understand the purpose and value of an IRP, it is also important to examine what the IRP is not. The IRP is not a
request for approval of a near-term construction plan, and it does not authorize specific projects, programs, or cost
recovery. Instead, it is a planning document that represents a snapshot in time, based on current laws, policies,
technology, cost assumptions, and normal weather conditions, and is updated with each annual filing.

2.1.1 A Note on Timing and Emerging IRP Legislation
Dominion Energy is required to file an IRP, either a full IRP or an IRP update, every year in Virginia and North
Carolina. In the past, the Company was required to file a full IRP with the SCC and NCUC in even numbered years,
like it did in 2024. Due to new Virginia legislation (House Bill 429 and Senate Bill 249 (“HB 429/SB 249”) that was
signed into law in April 2026, however, the cadence of filing full IRPs changed for the Company’s submission to the
SCC. For Virginia, the Company is now required to file a full IRP in 2027, and then triennially thereafter (i.e., next full
IRP filing in Virginia after 2027 will be in 2030). Therefore, this year’s IRP is considered an update in Virginia. The
intent of an IRP update is to provide a “narrative summary describing any significant event necessitating a major
revision to the most recently filed [full] IRP, including adjustments to the type and size of resources identified.” 1
There is no change to the filing cadence in North Carolina, and therefore, this year’s IRP is considered a full IRP in
North Carolina. The Company files the 2026 IRP as an IRP update with the SCC in Virginia and full IRP with the
NCUC in North Carolina, consistent with all relevant laws, regulations, and commission orders.
The new Virginia legislation also expanded the scope of the IRP to include transmission and distribution, formally
extended the planning horizon to 20 years, and established more defined requirements around modeling, portfolio
development, and the evaluation of demand-side and grid-related resources. It also formalized additional
components of the stakeholder engagement process. While these new IRP requirements apply beginning in 2027,
this 2026 IRP addresses several of them, as noted below in Section 2.2.
In addition to the new Virginia legislation expanding the scope and changing the cadence of IRP filings, the Virginia
General Assembly enacted other legislation in 2026 that impacts the development of an IRP. House Bill 895 and
Senate Bill 448 (“HB 895/SB 448”), among other things, significantly expanded the size and extended the timeline of
the energy storage development targets for the Commonwealth. Under the new targets, the Company must petition
the SCC for approval to construct or acquire 16,000 MW of short-duration energy storage capacity by December 31,
2045, 4,000 MW of which must be petitioned for by December 31, 2030. HB 895/SB 448 also requires the Company
to petition for approval to construct, acquire, or procure 4,000 MW of long-duration energy storage capacity, half of

 Chapter 3: About Dominion Energy

3.1 Commitment to Reliability
Dominion Energy, as a regulated public electric utility, has an obligation to reliably serve all customers who request
service within its service territory. Practically, this means that the Company must have sufficient resources and
reserves to instantaneously respond to hourly, daily, and seasonal spikes in customer demand against the backdrop
of a steadily growing energy need in the Company’s service territory and within the region. As a vertically integrated
utility by state law, the Company operates all three aspects of electric utility service to serve customers: generation,
transmission, and distribution systems. The Company’s service territory is served by the Dominion Energy Load
Serving Entity (“DOM LSE”).
Dominion Energy’s generation portfolio consists of 21,026 MW of generation capacity, including approximately
1,912 MW of resources owned by third parties from which the Company purchases the output through power
purchase agreements (“PPAs”). The Company’s power generation resources create electricity from primary energy
sources, including nuclear, natural gas, coal, biomass, solar, wind, and water. The Company’s demand-side
management (“DSM”) portfolio consists of energy efficiency and demand response programs in Virginia and North
Carolina. The DSM portfolio offers voluntary energy conservation programs for customers that are designed to
reduce demand during peak periods.
Dominion Energy also owns and operates a portion of the transmission system (also known as the bulk power
system) that moves large amounts of electricity over long distances. This transmission system is responsible for
providing service (i) for redelivery to the Company’s retail customers in Virginia and North Carolina; (ii) to Old
Dominion Electric Cooperative, Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative (“NOVEC”), Central Virginia Electric


                                                          10
 Cooperative, and Virginia Municipal Electric Association for redelivery to their retail customers in Virginia; and, (iii) to
North Carolina Electric Membership Corporation and North Carolina Eastern Municipal Power Agency for redelivery
to their customers in North Carolina (collectively, this region is referred to as the DOM Zone and encompasses the
DOM LSE as well as the territories of other LSEs). Dominion Energy owns approximately 6,800 miles of
transmission lines at voltages ranging from 69 kilovolts (“kV”) to 500 kV in Virginia, North Carolina, and West
Virginia.
The DOM Zone is part of PJM, 2 which encompasses all or part of 13 states, as well as the District of Columbia. PJM
is part of the larger Eastern Interconnection transmission grid, meaning the transmission system is interconnected,
directly or indirectly, with other transmission systems in the United States and Canada between the Rocky
Mountains and the Atlantic Coast, except for Quebec and most of Texas (the “Eastern Interconnection”). The
transmission systems in the Eastern Interconnection depend on each other for moving bulk power through the
transmission system and for reliability support. Accordingly, as a transmission owner, Dominion Energy is not only
responsible for reliable service to its own transmission customers, but also contributes to the integrity of the Eastern
Interconnection as a whole.
Additionally, Dominion Energy owns approximately 61,000 miles of distribution lines at voltages ranging from 4 kV to
46 kV in Virginia and North Carolina. Distribution lines deliver power from substations to individual neighborhoods,
homes, and businesses.
Dominion Energy must plan and operate its three functional aspects to ensure reliability for all customers. For power
generation, reliability requires sufficient generation resources and resource diversity to avoid over-reliance on any
one energy source, along with dependable fuel supplies. The generation portfolio must be able to meet both real-
time demand for electricity and PJM reserve requirements (i.e., the need to have sufficient generation on standby).
While Dominion Energy operates a diverse portfolio of resources and engages in necessary market purchases to
serve customers’ energy and capacity needs, the ability to purchase power is finite, and over-reliance on market
purchases will create risks to both reliability and affordability.
The reliability of the transmission system depends on a number of factors, with North American Electric Reliability
Corporation (“NERC”) Reliability Standards being one of the major drivers. Responsibly siting, building, and utilizing
transmission lines allows customers to be confident they will reliably receive energy at their homes and businesses.
NERC Reliability Standards set baseline thresholds to ensure that the transmission system is reliably planned and
operated. The Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”), managed by PJM for its members, allows for
efficient and reliable transmission planning.
Electric operations continue to focus on improving service and experience levels while striving to reduce costs.
System Average Interruption Duration Index, or SAIDI, is a metric used to measure electric service reliability. SAIDI
performance results, excluding major events, were 133 minutes for the three-year average ending in 2025, up from
the previous three-year average of 130 minutes. This increase is primarily due to increased storm activity.
Dominion Energy has a strong track record of reliability for its Virginia and North Carolina territory over the last five
years, demonstrating that, excluding major storms, customers have uninterrupted electric service 99.98% of the time
throughout the year. This record reflects both the Company’s strengths as an operator of power distribution assets
and the Company’s investments in the reliability of its distribution system.

 3.2 Commitment to Affordability
Dominion Energy provides electric service at affordable and competitive rates to residential, commercial, and
industrial customers. Our electric rates continue to compare favorably to national and regional average electric rates
on both a current and historical basis. Based on its latest projections of electric rates in the forward-looking bill
analysis, the Company expects to maintain its long record of competitive rates.
Customer Protections
The past two years have seen important developments in the Company’s commitment to ensuring all customers pay
fair and equitable shares to support electric grid investments.
In December 2024, the Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission released the results of a year-long
study of data center industry impacts in Virginia. The results concluded that data centers had been paying their full
cost of electric service but foreshadowed that additional reforms could be necessary to ensure fairness going
forward.
To ensure data centers and other high load customers continue to pay their fair share and to mitigate against
stranded costs, the Company proposed, and the SCC approved, a robust package of cost allocation, rate design,
and Terms and Conditions changes in the Company’s biennial review proceeding, Case No. PUR-2025-00058.
Notably, the Company’s proposals included the creation of a new customer class for its most energy-intensive
customers. The criteria for inclusion in the new class (called GS-5) are: 1) a contracted or measured electric
demand equal to or greater than 25 megawatts, and 2) an anticipated or measured electric load factor of 75% or
more. While data centers generally fit this profile of high demand paired with a high load factor, the new GS-5 class
is not exclusive to data centers. Any customer that meets both criteria will take service under GS-5 on and after
January 1, 2027, except for customers meeting certain employment provisions that exercise(d) a one-time opt-out
provision provided for under Virginia law. 3
When determining electric rates, it is important to examine both the costs that are eligible to be recovered from the
Company’s customers and how those costs should be allocated among customer classes. By concentrating the
most energy-intensive users in the GS-5 class, the Company will enable greater transparency and precision when
those cost-allocation decisions are made.
In addition to authorizing the creation of the GS-5 class, the SCC also approved a package of new and strengthened
contractual provisions for high-load customers including long-term contracts, minimum charges, collateral
requirements, and exit fees. With limited exceptions, they apply to all customers, individually or on contiguous
property, under any rate schedule with actual or contracted electric demand greater than or equal to 25 megawatts.
These provisions protect residential and other customers from bearing infrastructure costs driven by high-load
customers. They function by creating binding financial commitments, which ensure that high-load customers
continue paying their fair share of electric utility infrastructure costs.
Effective January 2027, high-load customers will face minimum charges that set a floor for what they pay, which is

4.1 PJM Market Considerations
Updates to the PJM Market Affect the Planning Environment
Dominion Energy participates in the PJM capacity planning process and capacity auctions to ensure supply of
sufficient capacity resources to meet its customer load. As a member of PJM, the Company has two options to meet
its capacity requirements: (1) participation in the reliability pricing model (“RPM”) forward capacity market, or (2)
utilization of the fixed resource requirement (“FRR”) alternative. Dominion Energy currently participates in the first
option, the RPM capacity market. The RPM is PJM’s resource adequacy construct, and its purpose is to procure
sufficient resources to ensure reliability across the Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) while developing a
long-term pricing signal for capacity resources within each Locational Deliverability Area (“LDA”). The PJM LDA for

                                                          18
 the Company is the equivalent of the DOM Zone. Under the RPM, entities participate in PJM auctions to meet
capacity obligations through a clearing mechanism that uses a pre-defined demand curve and clears offered
generation supply resources against that demand curve.
Capacity Planning
As a member of PJM, Dominion Energy is a signatory to PJM’s Reliability Assurance Agreement, which obligates
the Company to purchase sufficient capacity to maintain overall system reliability. PJM determines these obligations
for each zone using its annual load forecast and reserve margin 5 guidelines as inputs. PJM then conducts a
capacity auction process for meeting these input requirements up to three years into the future. This auction process
includes the Base Residual Auction (“BRA”) for the RPM as well as subsequent incremental auctions that are held
to allow market sellers and PJM to adjust positions for changes such as load forecasts, generator retirements,
ELCC, construction delays, or outage assumptions. This auction process determines the clearing reserve margin
and the capacity price for each zone for the delivery year that is three years in the future.
The Company is required to provide sufficient generation to cover its load obligation, which is calculated using
PJM’s most current load forecast and planning parameters such as ELCC, reserve margin requirements, and
transmission import limitations.
Dominion Energy uses PJM’s reserve margin guidelines to determine its long-term capacity requirement. PJM
conducts an annual reserve requirement study to determine an adequate level of capacity in its footprint to meet the
target level of reliability, measured as a loss of load expectation equivalent to one day of outage in ten years.
PJM develops reserve margin estimates for planning (i.e., delivery) years (June through May) rather than calendar
years. Because PJM is a summer peaking entity, and because the summer period of PJM’s planning year coincides
with the calendar year summer period, calendar and planning year reserve requirement estimates are determined
based on the identical summer period. For example, the Company uses PJM’s 2026/2027 delivery year
assumptions for the 2026 calendar year in this 2026 IRP because it represents the expected peak load during the
summer of 2026.

 4.1.1 The 2028/2029 PJM BRA Results
On July 14, 2026, PJM published the results of the BRA for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year. The results showed that
the entire PJM footprint again cleared at the FERC-approved capacity price cap, with a clearing price of
$325.00/MW-day, a modest 2.5% decrease from the $333.44/MW-day clearing price established in the 2027/2028
BRA. 6 Similar to the prior auction, the DOM Zone did not separate from the remainder of PJM, and no other PJM
load deliverability areas experienced price separation.
Despite the relatively small change in clearing price, the 2028/2029 BRA reinforced concerns regarding PJM’s long-
term supply-demand balance. PJM procured 138,317.8 MW of unforced capacity (“UCAP”) through the RPM
auction, while an additional 10,863.8 MW of UCAP was supplied through the FRR construct, resulting in total
committed resources of 149,181.6 MW UCAP. However, PJM determined that its reliability requirement for the
Delivery Year was approximately 156,013 MW UCAP, leaving the region over 6,800 MW below the resource level
needed to satisfy PJM’s one-in-ten-year reliability standard. This marked the second consecutive auction in which
PJM was effectively unable to procure sufficient resources to meet its target reliability requirement and represented
the second auction in which the entire RTO fell materially short of the planning reserve target.
The shortfall was driven largely by continued growth in forecasted electricity demand, particularly from large load
additions and data center development, which increased PJM’s reliability requirement by more than 3,600 MW
relative to the prior auction. PJM reported that supply offered into the capacity market increased by approximately
3,447 MW UCAP, while forecasted load increased by 1,375 MW.
The 2028/2029 BRA also highlighted the growing gap between PJM’s IRM requirement and the level of capacity
ultimately committed through the auction. PJM’s reliability studies indicated that an IRM of 20.0% was necessary to
maintain the one-day-in-ten-year Loss of Load Expectation reliability standard for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.
However, the auction cleared at an IRM of 14.4%, or 5.6% below that target. The widening gap reflects the
combined effects of accelerating load growth, resource accreditation changes under ELCC methodologies, and the
cumulative impact of more than a decade of thermal unit retirements, with replacement resource additions and
accreditation not fully offsetting those losses. While recent PJM and stakeholder initiatives have increasingly
focused on reforming reliability planning assumptions, accreditation methodologies, and market design constructs,
current auction results highlight the fundamental challenge PJM faces in maintaining adequate reserve margins
across the region.
PJM estimated that absent the FERC-approved price cap, the auction would have cleared at approximately
$554.72/MW-day. 7 While actual auction outcomes without the cap cannot be known with certainty, these estimates
highlight the continued scarcity of accredited capacity resources across the PJM footprint and the increasing value
of reliable generation capable of contributing to system adequacy.
For Dominion Energy, the 2028/2029 BRA results reinforce the importance of maintaining and developing
accredited capacity resources within the Company’s service territory. Continued load growth coupled with
dispatchable generation retirements, increasing reserve requirements, and evolving ELCC accreditation
methodologies have driven PJM-wide capacity shortages and a growing divergence between procured capacity and
system reliability requirements. As a net importer of energy and a region with PJM’s highest projected load growth,
the DOM Zone currently remains dependent on sufficient generating resources both within and outside the
Company’s footprint. These results support the importance of continued evaluation of generation additions, storage,
demand-side resources, transmission enhancements, and market purchases as part of Dominion Energy’s long-
term resource planning process.

 4.1.2 Resource Adequacy and Market Functioning Challenges in PJM
Capacity Market
Section 56-599 of the Code of Virginia (“Va. Code”) requires every IRP to consider energy independence along with
rate stability, economic development, and service reliability. PJM is responsible for finding the least cost means of
satisfying demand while meeting reliability requirements, and dispatches power generators within the entire RTO
accordingly. Dominion Energy works with PJM to satisfy its requirements through load procurement in the PJM
market. The Company also coordinates with PJM on power generation in the operational space through day-ahead
offering of its generating units into the market and real-time dispatch of the units.
Even though PJM dispatches generators within its entire footprint to meet its load requirements, Dominion Energy is
responsible for responding to its customers’ demand growth. The Company must adjust to load shape changes in its
service territory (i.e., shifts in the timing of demand highs and lows), which requires appropriate dispatch and
resource mix adjustments. Dominion Energy meets demand for electric service with a combination of its
dispatchable units, renewable and energy storage resources, and market purchases.
The Company has depended upon market power purchases for an increasing share of total energy served,
purchasing between 20 to 23% of total energy in 2021-2025, and this number continues to grow. While market
purchases have historically been a part of meeting customers’ needs, the Company aims to be less reliant on
generation outside of the DOM Zone, as an overdependence on market purchases is a growing cause for concern
for several reasons.
As discussed in The 2028/2029 PJM BRA Results section, these challenges were reflected in the results of PJM's
recent Base Residual Auctions. In both auctions, the PJM-wide capacity market cleared at the FERC-approved
capacity price cap, and PJM was unable to procure sufficient accredited capacity resources to fully satisfy its
reliability requirement. These results demonstrate that the resource adequacy challenges facing PJM are no longer
isolated to specific zones but instead represent a broader regional concern.
The entire PJM region is experiencing unprecedented load growth, which results in challenges in securing capacity
resources needed to meet that growing demand. This challenge is exacerbated by (i) significant loss of dispatchable
generation capacity throughout PJM due to premature retirements, and (ii) the composition of PJM's interconnection
queue that continues to be dominated by solar, wind, energy storage, and hybrid resources, while comparatively
fewer new dispatchable thermal resources are advancing through the queue. 8 As reserves decline, the safety
cushion that is essential for reliability shrinks and power may not be available when it is needed, particularly during
extreme weather events or other demand spikes.
A significant portion of PJM's forecasted load growth is associated with large-load additions, particularly data
centers and other energy-intensive customers. In response, PJM has undertaken several initiatives to refine load
forecasting methodologies, improve how large-load additions are assessed, forecasted, and incorporated into
planning studies, and evaluate mechanisms that better align new load additions with available generation and
transmission infrastructure. PJM and stakeholders continue to evaluate policies related to load forecasting accuracy,
customer commitment requirements, curtailment provisions, and alternative approaches that may allow certain large
loads to coordinate generation development with load additions. These efforts reflect growing recognition that the
magnitude and pace of forecasted demand growth introduce additional uncertainty into long-term resource
adequacy planning and may materially influence future capacity requirements, transmission expansion needs, and
market outcomes.
In addition to growing demand, PJM has implemented changes to its resource adequacy framework. ELCC
accreditation now serves as the primary methodology for determining the reliability contribution of generation,
storage, demand response, and renewable resources. ELCC better reflects the actual contribution of resources
during reliability events but has reduced accredited capacity values for certain technologies relative to previous

PJM has also increased its focus on winter reliability risks. Following several extreme weather events and updated
reliability studies, PJM's resource adequacy framework now places greater emphasis on winter performance and
correlated outage risks. Indeed, resource planning must assess both summer and winter reliability needs,
particularly as growing portions of future resources consist of weather-dependent resources whose availability

Another indicator of resource adequacy concerns is the increasing reliance of PJM LDAs on imported capacity
during system emergencies. PJM measures this through the Capacity Emergency Transfer Objective (“CETO”),
which represents the amount of imported capacity an LDA is expected to require under emergency conditions.
CETO reflects the balance between local supply and demand, with higher values indicating greater reliance on
imported capacity during system emergencies. Increasing CETO values therefore indicate a growing dependence
on external resources to meet peak demand during extreme weather events.
CETO metrics across the PJM region continue to trend upward, reflecting the combined impacts of load growth,
generation retirements, and transmission constraints. At the same time, neighboring regions that have historically
provided surplus capacity are facing their own resource adequacy challenges. Thus, the availability of imported
capacity during periods of system stress is becoming increasingly uncertain, raising concerns about the ability of
affected LDAs to maintain reliability during extreme conditions.
While PJM markets will continue to play an important role in meeting customer needs, recent market outcomes raise
questions regarding the ability of the RPM construct alone to support development of the resources needed for long-
term reliability. Capacity markets were originally intended to procure residual capacity needs after utilities and
market participants secured most requirements through ownership and bilateral contracting arrangements. Over
time, increasing reliance on the BRA as a primary procurement mechanism has resulted in significantly higher
capacity prices without necessarily providing the long-term revenue certainty required to support investment in
capital-intensive dispatchable generation resources, many of which require development timelines that exceed the
auction’s three-year forward horizon.
The BRA was designed as a market to procure residual capacity. In that regard, PJM envisioned that LDAs would
secure their capacity by building resources themselves or procuring them with bilateral contracts and use the BRA
to manage relatively modest long or short positions. Over time, however, LDAs have increasingly used the BRA as
the primary place to obtain needed capacity. When load growth increased at an accelerated rate and dispatchable
generation continued to retire, the utilization of the BRA as a place to procure needed capacity resulted in a
dramatic increase in capacity prices. This, in turn, signals the need for new generation to be built. Compounding the
issue, though, is the fact that the BRA is not designed to support the needed power generation development.
Because the BRA only establishes prices for capacity to be delivered three years in the future and dispatchable
capacity resources, like natural gas-fired or nuclear resources, cannot be built in a short three-year timeframe, the
BRA does not provide a market result that is capable of matching supply and demand for all the types of needed
capacity or the long-term revenue certainty needed to incentivize development of capital-intensive capacity
resources.
PJM, stakeholders, and regulators have increasingly focused on whether the existing RPM construct provides
sufficient incentives to support investment in the quantity and types of resources needed to maintain long-term
reliability. Ongoing discussions include evaluation of the interaction between energy, ancillary services, and capacity
markets, potential enhancements to market design, and mechanisms that could provide greater revenue certainty
for new resource development. While no final reforms have been adopted, continued market design discussions
introduce uncertainty regarding future capacity procurement structures, accreditation methodologies, and long-term
capacity pricing.
Transmission expansion remains an important component of maintaining reliability and reducing market constraints.
PJM continues to advance major transmission projects intended to improve power transfers, facilitate resource
integration, and alleviate deliverability limitations. While transmission expansion can improve power transfers and

 reduce congestion, it cannot fully address resource adequacy concerns absent sufficient regional generation
resources. The effectiveness of transmission expansion therefore remains closely linked to the development and
retention of reliable generation resources both within PJM and across the Eastern Interconnection.
Dominion Energy continues to pursue a broad range of strategies to ensure reliable and affordable service for
customers. These strategies include development of new generation resources, expansion of renewable energy and
energy storage facilities, execution of power purchase agreements, transmission and distribution enhancements,
grid-enhancing technologies, fuel assurance planning, demand-side management programs, energy efficiency
initiatives, and prudent participation in wholesale energy and capacity markets.
While market purchases will remain an important component of serving customer load, current PJM market
conditions underscore the value of maintaining a balanced portfolio of Company-owned and contracted resources.
Continued load growth, declining reserve margins, evolving accreditation methodologies, and ongoing generator
retirements support the need for additional accredited capacity within the Company’s service territory. A diverse mix
of dispatchable generation, renewable resources, energy storage, transmission investments, and demand-side
programs provides the flexibility necessary to maintain reliability and manage long-term customer costs.
Resource Adequacy
Resource adequacy is the ability of the electric system to supply the aggregate energy requirements of electricity to
consumers at all times, taking into account scheduled and reasonably expected unscheduled outages of generation
and transmission facilities. Today, diverse resource fleets across the Eastern Interconnection generally allow for
power exchanges between PJM and its neighboring RTOs, although extreme weather can challenge the stability of
the Eastern Interconnection absent significant new investments.
To meet the growing demand, the Company makes infrastructure investments in its generation, transmission, and
distribution systems. The Company and PJM continue to study the impacts of increasing penetration of renewable
generation on reliability of the bulk electric system. Renewable energy resources are not a one-for-one replacement
for traditional dispatchable generation resources. Generally, more installed capacity of solar and energy storage
resources is necessary to equate to the capacity and energy that traditional generation provides. A flexible and
diverse portfolio that includes dispatchable, renewable, and energy storage resources, as well as enhanced
coordination across the Eastern Interconnection will be needed to maintain system balancing and ramping needs
and to ensure system reliability.

4.1.4 Reserve Requirements
Reserve requirements ensure that enough resources are available to reliably operate the system when unusual
conditions occur. Balancing Authorities, such as PJM, establish reserve requirements based on NERC Reliability
Standards. Both operating and planning reserves are required to maintain system reliability. Different types of
resources provide different types of reserves. For instance, traditional dispatchable and energy storage resources
can provide operating reserves, but renewable resources generally cannot. Therefore, a diverse mix of generation
resources is needed to ensure reserve requirements are met.

The Company performed the analyses in this 2026 IRP using energy and commodity price forecasts provided by

hours, seasons, and operating conditions.


4.5.2.1 Challenges in Solar Development
The scale and pace of solar deployment contemplated in long-term planning must be evaluated against a growing
set of practical development constraints. Solar development is increasingly shaped not only by resource need, but
also by whether projects can be sited, permitted, approved, interconnected, and constructed in a manner that
supports customer value and maintains system reliability. In that regard, key constraints are discussed further
below.
Land Availability, Land-use Conditions, and Permitting
Land availability and local land-use conditions are increasingly material constraints for solar development. While
utility-scale solar can provide large blocks of energy and economies of scale in project development, it also requires
significant acreage of land suitable for development, cost-effective interconnection, satisfaction of environmental
and permitting requirements, and ability to obtain required local approvals.
Community support is a key factor or constraint in solar development. Local governments have legitimate interests
in land-use planning, tax impacts, community character, and long-term land stewardship. Through local ordinances,
the permitting process, and zoning decisions, localities set requirements for, among other things, viewsheds,
buffers, vegetation management, stormwater management, agricultural preservation, construction traffic, and
decommissioning. However, cumulative local restrictions can narrow the universe of viable project sites, increase
competition and costs, delay development, and materially affect the Company’s ability to develop or acquire solar
projects at the pace and scale assumed in long-term planning.


                                                            35
 Successful solar development depends on early and meaningful engagement with local communities, landowners,
public officials, and other stakeholders. Community support, or opposition can significantly affect project outcomes.
The Company continues to work collaboratively with local governments and stakeholders to identify and carefully
design projects to better position them to advance through the local approval process.
Previously developed and distributed solar sites, such as rooftops, carports, and landfills, provide an important
complement to utility-scale solar by reducing greenfield land impacts and supporting statutory objectives related to
development on previously developed lands. These projects provide benefits such as the ability to site generation
closer to load and more siting flexibility. They can also create opportunities for visible partnerships with local
governments, public institutions, commercial customers, and other host-site owners.
However, these projects provide their own unique challenges and are often more complex than conventional
ground-mounted solar. They may require more intensive diligence, greater host-site coordination, and more
customized engineering. For instance, such projects may require additional structural, environmental, and/or
geotechnical reviews; pose operational and maintenance challenges due to rooftop age, replacement, or warranties;
cause access and timing constraints for construction and ongoing operations given the primary use of the site; and
often require complex commercial arrangements with the site host. Additionally, these projects are typically higher
cost due to their smaller size and specialized design requirements.
Interconnection and Transmission Planning Constraints
Interconnection, transmission planning, and locational value are key considerations and potential constraints in solar
development. As solar penetration increases, the most favorable interconnection locations may become more
limited. Recent experience has demonstrated that interconnection costs for required transmission or distribution
upgrades to safely connect new generation can make a project uneconomic. In addition to cost-effective
interconnection, the location of the facility in relation to existing distribution or transmission infrastructure, and

4.5.3 Storage Resources
Battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) offer significant benefits for grid operations, including enhanced flexibility,
reliability, supporting integration of variable renewable resources, and shifting energy in time to meet peak loads.
These advantages, combined with rapidly declining costs and the development of mature global supply chains, have
positioned BESS as a complementary resource in the evolving electricity grid.

4.5.3.1 Current State of Battery Energy Storage Deployment
Lithium-ion (“Li-ion”) technology dominates the market today, representing nearly all new utility-scale storage
deployments due to its proven performance, high energy density, and favorable economics compared to other
storage technologies.
Over the past decade, Li-ion systems have experienced one of the fastest cost declines of any energy technology—
falling by approximately 90% since 2010 14—enabling widespread adoption across both power and mobility sectors.
This cost trajectory, coupled with growing manufacturing scale and established supply chains, has made Li-ion the
preferred technology for near-term deployment, particularly for 2-to-4-hour duration applications. This trend is
reflected in the rapid growth of the U.S. energy storage market. In 2025 alone, the United States installed a record
18.9 GW of energy storage capacity, with utility-scale projects accounting for the majority of deployments. 15
Within this context, the Company has advanced a growing portfolio of energy storage assets, with over 170 MW of
Company-owned BESS projects approved and approximately 50 MW currently in operation. Additionally, 459 MW of
energy storage capacity has been approved under PPAs demonstrating a diversified procurement strategy that
balances ownership and third-party development. These projects provide critical grid services including peak
shaving, capacity contribution, and renewable integration.
Recent Virginia legislation substantially increased the Company’s energy storage deployment target. The Company
is now required to petition for 4,000 MW of short-duration energy storage capacity by 2030. Achieving this scale will
require coordinated planning across development, interconnection, procurement, and construction functions,
alongside continued adaptation to evolving market conditions. The Company continues to assess opportunities to
develop energy storage projects at existing generation facilities, including solar and fossil generation assets.

Long-duration energy storage (“LDES”) technologies offer extended discharge durations compared to conventional
Li-ion batteries. These systems fall into three primary categories based on their design: (1) thermal, (2)

efficiency; durability and degradation; safety and operational limitations; and siting. Additionally, LDES developers
face commercialization hurdles including value proposition (cost, performance metrics, and value of integration into

4.5.3.3 Challenges for Energy Storage Deployment
Interconnection Constraints
The PJM interconnection process represents one of the most significant barriers to timely storage deployment.

4.5.6 Natural Gas Resources
Natural gas resources are essential for grid reliability and the energy transition because they are dispatchable
resources that work in tandem with intermittent renewable generation. Their flexible operating characteristics allow
them to follow load and generate electricity when it is needed, including during periods of peak demand or when
renewable resources are unavailable. Natural gas units can quickly start, ramp output up or down, and shut off as
conditions change, helping to balance large swings in renewable energy production and mitigating the risk of
intermittent generation to maintain a reliable electric grid.
As baseload demand continues to grow, additional generation resources will be needed to ensure the electric
system can reliably meet increasing customer energy requirements. Rising demand places greater pressure on
existing generation assets and reduces the margin available to respond to peak conditions, equipment outages, or
fluctuations in renewable energy output. Expanding generation capacity, particularly with dispatchable resources
that can operate when needed, will help maintain grid reliability, support projected load growth, and ensure
adequate energy is available under a wide range of operating conditions.
For future new natural gas facilities, the Company is considering using advanced-class gas turbines to leverage
their significant advantages because they deliver higher efficiency, lower fuel consumption, and lower emissions


                                                           41
 than traditional turbine technologies. By producing more electricity from the same amount of natural gas, advanced-
class units reduce operating costs and improve market competitiveness, particularly for a baseload facility. Higher
efficiency also lowers carbon emissions per megawatt-hour, helping support environmental and regulatory
objectives while maximizing the value of available pipeline gas capacity. Advanced-class turbines are well suited for
large-scale combined-cycle configurations because their higher output allows a plant to achieve maximum output
with fewer generating units, reducing overall plant complexity and maintenance requirements.
The Company is currently considering a combined-cycle (“CC”) approach for new baseload natural gas generation
facilities. A CC power plant is typically the preferred choice when the system needs a large amount of reliable,
dispatchable energy that will run frequently throughout the year. Unlike a simple-cycle combustion turbine (“CT”), a
CC plant captures the exhaust heat from the gas turbines and uses it to produce steam that drives a steam turbine,
generating additional electricity from the same fuel. This significantly improves efficiency, reduces fuel costs, and
lowers emissions per megawatt-hour.
CTs are generally developed when the primary need is peaking capacity, rapid startup capability, or operational
flexibility rather than low-cost energy production. They are less expensive to construct, can be brought online more
quickly, and are well suited for serving peak demand periods, supporting renewable integration, and maintaining
reliability during extreme weather events. For that reason, facilities such as the Chesterfield Energy Reliability
Center are being developed with simple-cycle CT technology to provide flexible reliability support, while larger
combined-cycle projects are intended to meet the system’s growing energy requirements over the long term.
To meet the energy and capacity needs associated with the load forecast, and in the absence of a commercially
viable carbon-free, dispatchable generation alternative, natural gas generation will remain a critical component of
the Company's strategy to reliably meet generation demand.

As society becomes increasingly dependent on electricity, customers expect higher levels of reliability, resiliency,

4.8 Environmental Considerations
Environmental regulation remains a key focus in long-term resource planning. Federal and state requirements
affecting the electric generating sector continue to evolve through rulemaking, reconsideration, litigation, or other
administrative action.
Coal-fired, biomass, and natural gas-fired generation continue to support system reliability. Natural gas-fired units,
particularly simple-cycle combustion turbines, can respond quickly during periods of high demand. Coal and
biomass units may provide additional operational resilience because they can maintain onsite fuel inventories when
regional fuel supplies are constrained or curtailed, including during peak winter conditions. State and federal
developments may affect the dispatch, economics, compliance obligations, and continued operation of these
resources.
Several federal regulatory programs are particularly relevant to the Company’s fossil-fueled generating fleet. These
include the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards rule applicable to coal electric generating units; greenhouse gas
standards, and emission guidelines established under Sections 111(b) and 111(d) of the Clean Air Act; Effluent
Limitation Guidelines for wastewater discharges; and Virginia’s CO2 Budget Trading Program, which implements the
Commonwealth’s participation in RGGI.

 5.3 Locational Model
In its Final Order in Case No. PUR-2024-00184 (the 2024 IRP), the SCC directed that "[i]n modeling Dominion’s
next IRP, Dominion and [VA] Staff shall work together to develop a locational model in PLEXOS using no more than
four (4) Virginia-specific regional nodes." 22 Consistent with that directive, the Company has developed a locational
modeling framework and presents the results of that effort in this 2026 IRP.
The Company engaged in a series of collaborative discussions with VA Staff, including alignment on the scope and
design of the locational model. As agreed with VA Staff, the locational model applies four nodes to a single portfolio:
(1) DOM LSE North, (2) DOM LSE South, (3) non-DOM LSE/PJM market node to the north (“Market North”), and
non-DOM LSE/PJM market node to the south (“Market South”), with the James River serving as the conceptual
dividing line. Transfers among these nodes are constrained by three transmission “pipes,” and the analysis
incorporates zonal build limits and the PJM-derived DOM LSE Load Forecast allocated between the northern and
southern zones based on the split forecast in the Company Load Forecast. The dividing line itself was refined to
include a transmission capacity study of major wires crossing between the zones and a GIS-based allocation of
load, including data center demand. PLEXOS was then used to model a resulting least-cost expansion plan.
The resulting 20-year expansion plan totals approximately 41.1 GW of new capacity through 2046. Relative to the
Company Preferred Plan, the locational model selects approximately 1,900 MW of additional energy storage—
concentrated in the South, where solar could otherwise be curtailed—one additional SMR in the North, and no
incremental onshore wind, while holding natural gas additions constant. These results, together with the underlying
assumptions, are described in the sections that follow.
Description of Locational Model
As noted above, the locational model uses a north-south dividing line primarily based on the major transmission
corridors that exist within DOM Zone. At a high level, that dividing line exists roughly along the path of the James
River. The final “line” is depicted in Figure 5-24: Locational Model Illustrative Visual.

6.1 Environmental Justice
The Company remains committed to making environmental justice (“EJ”) considerations part of our everyday
decision-making as we work to deliver reliable, affordable, and increasingly clean energy to our customers in
Virginia and North Carolina. The Company continues to follow its EJ policy and the Virginia Environmental Justice
Act (“VEJA”) in its reviews for all major projects.
Dominion Energy’s EJ Policy
In 2018, the Company adopted an EJ policy. Under this policy, project development teams are required to consult
with the Company’s dedicated EJ specialists who conduct EJ reviews for all major projects, regardless of whether it
is required for permitting or other regulatory approvals.
The Company’s EJ evaluations begin as early as feasible in the project development cycle. The Company identifies
potentially disadvantaged or marginalized segments of the community near a potential project site according to
statutory definitions and designs an outreach plan to equitably solicit meaningful feedback from all interested
community members. The Company’s outreach efforts include the project development and construction team,
communications staff, and permitting experts who all work together to ensure information is available, questions are
answered, and feedback from the community is considered.
The Company works closely with all appropriate federal, state, local, and tribal agencies to mitigate environmental
impacts through the required permitting, approval, or consultation processes.

 The Virginia Environmental Justice Act
The VEJA sets the policy of Virginia to promote EJ, ensuring the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of every
person—regardless of race, color, national origin, income, faith, or disability—regarding the development,
implementation, or enforcement of any environmental law, regulation, or policy.
Using data from VDEQ’s EJScreen+ website, a Company analysis finds VEJA definitions identify approximately
80% of the Commonwealth’s land area as meeting EJ community definitions, and approximately 86% of the
Commonwealth’s population currently live in an area of the Commonwealth that meets EJ community definitions.
With such a large proportion of the Commonwealth defined through the VEJA as an EJ Community, avoidance is
not possible. Figure 6-1: VEJA EJ Community Map with the Company’s Generation Resources shows the
Company’s generation resources along with the geographic areas that meet the definition of EJ community in 2026.

Considering Environmental Justice
Generally, evaluation of environmental justice involves consideration of a variety of case-specific factors, including
(1) the type of project or program at issue; (2) where it will occur; (3) what type of environmental impacts are likely;
(4) if any impacts, whether they are significantly negative or adverse; and, (5) whether there are EJ communities
that might suffer the adverse environmental impacts of the proposed activity. The Company follows its established

                                                           88
 EJ review process when evaluating specific projects and programs and presents the results of the review in the
relevant proceedings before the SCC. The Company will also present its evaluation as appropriate in relevant
proceedings before the NCUC.
Importantly, a reliable and affordable energy grid is essential to a healthy environment for any community, as are the
economic development opportunities contingent upon the same. The transition to a clean-energy future will require
substantial development of new infrastructure across the Commonwealth. The public need for new infrastructure
and the potential harm done by selecting a “no action,” more costly, or less reliable alternative must be weighed
against the possible outcomes for local communities resulting from any proposed project.
The Company believes that whether a proposed action promotes EJ is best evaluated on a case-by-case basis,
informed by the location of the project in question and project-specific characteristics. The Company has established
an EJ review process for evaluating its specific projects and programs consistent with relevant laws and regulations.
Based on this, the Company presents the results of these project-specific review processes in the relevant
proceedings before the SCC, such as in its applications to construct new generating facilities or new or rebuilt
transmission lines, and will do so as appropriate in relevant proceedings before the NCUC.
As demonstrated in this IRP, meeting customers’ needs will require an “All of the Above” strategy with a portfolio of

communities in which it operates continue.
